findings.situation: A filer receives a distribution from a Roth IRA that receives SEP contributions (a Roth SEP IRA) and must choose between traditional_ira, whose wording says it 'includes SEP', and roth_ira, which mentions only 'a Roth IRA or Roth SIMPLE IRA'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 26: "an IRA includes a traditional IRA (which includes a traditional IRA that receives contributions from a simplified employee pension (SEP) arrangement), Roth IRA (which includes a Roth IRA that receives contributions from a SEP arrangement)"
findings.why: The traditional_ira option says it 'includes SEP' without limiting this to traditional SEP IRAs, and the roth_ira option does not mention Roth SEP IRAs, so a Roth SEP holder could reasonably choose traditional_ira. That choice sets retirement.roth to false and sends the distribution down the traditional-IRA path instead of Exception 2, item 2, which changes line 4b.

findings.situation: A filer who also took a retirement or IRA distribution in 2023, in 2024, or in 2026 before the return's due date has those amounts left out of Form 8880 line 4, because box 1 of a 2025 Form 1099-R shows only 2025 distributions.
findings.source_text: f8880 p. 2, Line 4: "Enter the total amount of distributions you, and your spouse if filing jointly, received after 2022 and before the due date of your 2025 return (including extensions)"
findings.why: retirement.sav_gross feeds f8880.line4a from this year's box 1 only. Form 8880 line 4 needs a period of about three years, plus the part of 2026 before the due date, and no other question supplies those amounts.

findings.situation: A filer whose box 1 includes a Roth conversion, a distribution from an IRA inherited from someone other than a spouse, a loan treated as a distribution, a corrective distribution of excess contributions, military retirement pay, or section 404(k) dividends has that amount counted on Form 8880 line 4, even though the instructions exclude it.
findings.source_text: f8880 p. 2, Line 4: "Don't include any of the following. ... Distributions from your eligible retirement plan (other than a Roth IRA) rolled over or converted to your Roth IRA ... Loans from a qualified employer plan treated as a distribution ... Distributions of excess contributions or deferrals ... Distributions from a military retirement plan ... Distributions from an inherited IRA by a nonspousal beneficiary"
findings.why: The question asks for all of box 1 ("Gross distribution, Form 1099-R box 1"), and retirement.sav_gross takes off only the amount rolled over to a non-Roth account. So these excluded kinds of distribution stay in f8880.line4a.

findings.situation: A filer whose 1099-R reports a disability pension received before the employer's minimum retirement age, or a corrective distribution of excess deferrals, has box 1 placed on line 5a, 5b, or both, when it belongs on line 1h.

findings.why: Box 1 goes straight into retirement.smw1, annuity_taxable and plan_simple, and from there to lines 5a and 5b. Neither the question nor its help separates out these payments, and the listed refusals don't cover them.

findings.situation: A filer under 59½ receives a code 7 distribution from a governmental section 457 plan (not from a rollover) and answers yes because they were under 59½, although the additional tax does not apply and the code is not wrong.

findings.why: The wording treats being under 59½ as proof that code 7 is wrong. This brings in distributions that properly carry code 7 and owe no early-distribution tax, so they are refused unnecessarily.

findings.situation: A filer types a count above 12 (for example a typo, or counting each payment rather than each month), and the tool accepts it even though line 5 only allows the months a single year's payments can cover.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 29, Simplified Method Worksheet, line 5: 'Multiply line 4 by the number of months for which this year's payments were made.'
findings.why: This year's payments can only cover up to 12 months, but the accepted answer is 'a whole number, zero or more, with no upper bound'. A larger number would make line 5 too big and line 9 (Form 1040 line 5b) too small.

findings.situation: A pension pays monthly in arrears, so the payment received in January 2025 covers December 2024 and the December 2025 payment arrives in January 2026.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 29, line 5: 'the number of months for which this year's payments were made'; line 1: 'total pension or annuity payments from Form 1099-R, box 1'
findings.why: The question 'Number of months in 2025 for which payments were made' can be read as calendar months of 2025 (leaving out the December 2024 month paid in 2025, or counting December 2025 even though it was paid in 2026). It can also be read as the months covered by payments received in 2025, which is what line 5 needs to match line 1. The two readings can give different counts.

findings.situation: A filer whose annuity starting date was before 1987 truthfully reports the cost they have excluded tax free in 1987 and later years, which is a positive amount, but the worksheet skips line 6 for that filer, so the line needs no amount (zero).
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 29, SMW line 5: "If your annuity starting date was before 1987, skip lines 6 and 7 and enter this amount on line 8."; line 10: "Was your annuity starting date before 1987? Yes. STOP"; p575 p. 12: "If your annuity starting date is before 1987, you can continue to take your monthly exclusion for as long as you receive your annuity."
findings.why: The question "Amount, if any, recovered tax free in years after 1986" carries no instruction to enter zero or skip when the annuity starting date was before 1987, and its pointer to last year's line 10 does not apply to that filer. A truthful nonzero answer feeds SMW 6, then line 7 (line 2 minus line 6) and line 8 (smaller of 5 or 7). That can cut the exclusion the text says continues without a cost limit, and overstate line 5b.

findings.situation: A filer takes a distribution from a Roth IRA and rolls it into another Roth IRA within 60 days. The filer truthfully answers 0 because the question limits the count to 'an IRA other than a Roth IRA'.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 1: 'Enter the total distribution on line 4a if you rolled over part or all of the distribution from one: • Roth IRA to another Roth IRA, or • IRA (other than a Roth IRA) to a qualified plan or another IRA (other than a Roth IRA). Also check box 1 on line 4c.'
findings.why: Exception 1 also covers Roth IRA to Roth IRA rollovers, so lines 4b and 4c need the amount rolled over. The question's 'other than a Roth IRA' limit leaves it out, so line 4b is overstated and box 1 on line 4c stays unchecked.

findings.situation: A filer receives a distribution from a designated Roth account in a 401(k) and rolls it into a Roth IRA within 60 days. The filer answers 0 because the destination is a Roth account.
findings.source_text: p575 p. 24, Designated Roth accounts: 'You can roll over an eligible rollover distribution from a designated Roth account into another designated Roth account or a Roth IRA.' ... 'Because you rolled over the part of the distribution that could be included in gross income (income earned), none of the distribution is included in gross income.'; i1040gi p. 30: 'From that result, subtract the amount of the rollover.'
findings.why: A rollover from a designated Roth account to a Roth IRA is a tax-free rollover that line 5b must subtract and line 5c must flag. The question shuts out every Roth destination, so this amount is never counted.

findings.situation: A filer has a qualified plan loan offset after leaving a job and rolls the offset amount into an IRA more than 60 days later but before the return's due date. No waiver or frozen deposit applies, so the filer does not count it.
findings.source_text: p575 p. 23, Plan loan offset: 'if you have a qualified plan loan offset, you will have until the due date (including extensions) for your tax return for the tax year in which the offset occurs to complete your rollover.'
findings.why: The question allows only 60 days, a waiver or a frozen-deposit extension. It leaves out the longer deadline for qualified plan loan offsets, so a valid rollover is left off line 5b and line 5c.
